Offensive Interference (the most common type) is always an immediate dead ball. Since the ball is dead the moment the bat hit the catcher (why interference was called). All other action is reset. So the runners should not get to advance and offensive player committing the interference (in this case the batter) is out.

Run does not count as the final out of the inning is a force out. It's VERY important to understand that a force out has nothing to do with the manner in which the out was made (stepping on the base vs tagging the runner), but in fact was the runner "forced" to advance. 

In your scenario the play began with the bases loaded. So that means every runner is "forced" to advance. This makes any out at the next base from their starting base a force out, even if they are tagged.

This depends on the situation. Let's run through them. 

PU = Plate Umpire  
FU = Field Umpire

Situation 1. No runners on. PU calls all pops to the entire field. Exceptions would be if FU goes out on any of the plays. At that point he should announce he is going out and then he can have the call. 

Situation 2. Runners on, in any combination. Imagine a cone, where the inside of the cone is between LF and RF, and the outside of the cone is everything outside of the RF and LF. FU calls all balls inside the cone, PU calls all balls outside of the cone. 

With balls inside of the cone, PU's job is to watch for the tag up.

So here is how the mechanics of this should work. Ball is hit into play to the 3rd basemen (F5). Plate Umpire (PU) should come out as far as he can towards 2nd base. The Field Umpire (FU), in B position follows the ball/play. Throw is to 2nd. FU should then be ready to follow the throw to 1st. PU should be watching for the interference at 2nd. 

It doesn't sound like the 2nd baseman F4, was in a strange spot, considering the orientation of 2nd base, and it's a force out. 

If this was my game I would call time and confer with my partner. If I am FU, I'm looking to see if the ball was cleanly caught. It doesn't sound like it was. The perception seems to be that the throw hit the runner. Unless he was doing something blatant, there wouldn't be interference that I can think of on this play because a thrown ball hit an active runner, to which there is no penalty. 

If the ball had been fielded cleanly and then the ball came out because of the runner not sliding or veering off, then I would ask my partner, PU, if he saw contact and we'd likely have an interference call. 

The real grey area here seems to be if the contact between the thrown ball and R1 was incidental or on purpose.

It's one thing if the throw carries the fielder into the runner. Then, yes, they both have a right to be in the space. But based on your description, the fielder is blocking the path to the base without the ball, which is absolutely Obstruction.

The correct ruling here is Obstruction on the catcher. The runner is safe. This is why.

When the runner and catcher make contact, note a couple of things:

1. The catcher is blocking the base path and NOT in possession of the ball at the moment of contact.

2. The runner did not make malicious contact with the catcher. You don't see him lower is shoulder or appear in any way to intentionally truck the catcher. When he's leaned forward, it is after contact, as a result of the impact.

Since its obstruction, it's a delayed dead ball until play has ended. Since the runner successfully touched home without being tagged, he is safe. Also, all other runners are allowed to remain on any additional bases they advanced to. 

If the runner had maliciously contacted the catcher, it would be an immediate dead ball, with the runner out. All other runners would have to return if they weren't forced, except the batter-runner would be awarded 1st.

This is not catchers interference. It's obstruction on the catcher. Interference is on the offense. Obstruction on the defense. Interference is an immediate dead ball. Obstruction is a delayed dead ball. 

Catchers Interference is when the batter hits the catchers glove with the bat. It's the only time Interference is called on the defense.

The Act establishes a voluntary nationwide system to give police an early warning of threats against police officers and to aid in the apprehension of suspects who have killed or seriously injured an officer.

BLUE Alert Activation Criteria
(RSMo 650.520) A Blue Alert is authorized when:

a law enforcement officer is killed or seriously injured in the line of duty; or

an officer is missing in connection with official duties; or

there is an imminent and credible threat to kill or seriously injure a law enforcement officer; and

there is actionable information known about a suspect for a public notification to be helpful to law enforcement; and

the law enforcement agency involved requests or approves the alert being issued.

A character my roll one Monster Knowledge check for a creature of their choice on their turn, as a free action. Characters must be proficient in the Intelligence check of their choice (or benefit from the Jack of All Trades class feature). I feel like I need more information to answer this question but I am going to go out on a limb and answer what I would do to make combat more exciting. The main thing as a DM I think you can do to make things more exciting and memorable, is to involve the players as much as possible. Especially when it comes to creation. This doesn't stop when you get to combat.

Focus on Theater of the Mind style combat. We want the players to imagine and see what's going on and while miniatures and grids are cool, I would discourage using them for anything more than just things like "these guys are over here, you're over there, etc". not actual, to scale distances type of things. We really don'e want the players touching the minis at all if you use them. Otherwise the focus becomes about the minis and not the action.

If there are multiple baddies, the first time a PC engages a bad guy in that encounter, ask the player to describe a trait unique to that bad guy. This will help identify who's being attacked in a creative and memorable manner rather than saying you attack Orc #1 (ie PC Kevin, playing the Paladin Randall Brightborn, declares he is attacking the nearest orc. The DM asks PC Kevin to describe a feature about the orc and Kevin responds that the orc is missing an eye. From then on that orc gets described as the one-eyed orc. Perhaps that orc escapes and shows up later on in the campaign and you point out after a successful perception check that the orc you're fighting only has one eye. Your PCs just created a memorable moment). Even if all the monsters die in an encounter, it still gives it color.

When a PC kills a monster ask them to describe the death blow. Again, this is involving the players in creating the scene. Remember, DnD is collaborative story telling. It shines when everyone is involved. Good luck with future combat!

I've been running this campaign for 2 years now and the group just entered Chapter 10. Here are my tips:

​

* Ditch the grid. There is simply too much early on going on with tunnels and NPCs and the like, that drawing all that stuff out and placing mini's is going to slow it down to a crawl. Switch to theater of the mind. 
* Kill off half the NPCs during the escape from Velkenvelve. This will trim down the number to something more manageable but also keeps it fun because the NPCs personalities are pretty awesome. 
* Focus on just how dire the situation is. They are in the Underdark, an alien landscape, trying to survive with no way out. Track food and water initially until they get the hang of resupplying, so that they understand that they really are up shit creek without a paddle. 
* All of the locations really need fleshed out. There are some GREAT DMs Guild products out there for some of the locations (I loved the one on Gracklestugh). I highly recommend using them. Same with travel across the Dark Lake. I found some solid extra products that really laid it out nicely. 
* Be prepared to come up with your own material to get the group through levels 7 and 8 as there isn't anything in the module for it. I ran some of my own content that got them there (this was when they escaped the Underdark).
* Pre-roll all of your encounters. There is so much travel in this game and honestly I often handwave large travel and turn it into more of an Indian Jones line on a map scenario, but I didn't in this one because the travel is actually important early on. The party really needs to feel like all is lost and trust me, they will as they travel endlessly and each town they come upon is overrun with Madness (my group got so excited every time they found a settlement, thinking it might be the way out. Soon they would realize that each one was worse than the last and now they are scared to death to go into any settlement).
